summary: For ages 7-8, turn multiplication tables from a memorised list into a web of derivable facts and checkable patterns. Children derive a harder fact (8×7) from anchor facts they own (8×5 + 8×2 = 40 + 16 = 56) using an array split, use a pattern as a reasonableness check (multiples of 4 and 8 are even — is my answer even?), and describe/test the rule of a growing sequence ('add 50 each time') to predict onward terms. The core habit is deriving AND self-checking, plus probing what a pattern does and does not claim.
misconceptions: Skip-counts or guesses harder facts instead of deriving them from known ones (8×5 + 8×2)
Splits the derivation wrongly (8×5 + 2, forgetting to multiply the 2 by 8)
Accepts an unreasonable answer because the pattern check (multiples of 4 are even) isn't applied
Over-generalises a pattern from a few cases without testing, or reverses it wrongly (thinks every even number is a multiple of 4)

activities.title: Split an array to derive a hard fact
steps: Face 8×7 shown as an array 8 rows tall and 7 wide.
Cut the 7 into 5 and 2 (drag a divider, fold a paper array, or draw a line) so the array cleaves into an 8×5 block and an 8×2 block.
Read off 8×5 = 40 and 8×2 = 16, then combine the two blocks to get 56.

Try a different way to reach the same answer: 8×8 − 8 = 64 − 8 = 56 (take one group of 8 away from eight 8s). Compare which way you prefer and why — this uses one fewer group of 8, which is a different idea from cutting the 7 into 5 and 2.
activities.insight: A 'hard' table fact can be assembled from facts you already own; the array makes the decomposition (distributive idea) visible rather than relying on recall or skip-counting, and the 8×8 − 8 route is a distinct alternative strategy (adjusting from a near fact), not another split of the 7.

activities.title: Use a table pattern as a reasonableness check
steps: Shade the multiples of 4 (and of 8) on a multiplication grid or hundred square and observe that every one is even.
State the pattern as a check: 'a multiple of 4 must be even — is my answer even?'
Apply the check to a proposed product: given a candidate like an odd 'multiple of 4', decide whether it can be right and say why.
Estimate before computing: 'roughly how big should 8×7 be — between which two facts I know?' (between 8×5=40 and 8×8=64).
activities.insight: A noticed pattern is not just an observation — it becomes a tool you use to catch your own errors and judge whether an answer looks plausible (this check shows an answer is plausible, e.g. even and within range, not that it is exactly right).

activities.title: Describe and test a sequence rule
steps: Given a growing sequence (e.g. steps of +50 along a number line), describe the rule in words: 'add 50 each time'.
Predict several terms ahead — e.g. the term after 350 (400), and the one after that (450) — then verify by stepping along the number line.
Say how sure you are and how you could check a predicted term.
activities.insight: A clearly stated rule lets you predict beyond what you can see and then verify, which is the predict-and-check habit in a sequence context.

activities.title: Test the limits of a pattern (don't over-reverse it)
steps: Consider the claim 'all multiples of 4 are even' and agree it is true.
Now test the reverse: 'is every even number a multiple of 4?' Try 6 — it is even but not a multiple of 4.
State precisely what the rule claims and what it does not (every multiple of 4 is even, but not every even number is a multiple of 4).
activities.insight: A true pattern often does not reverse; testing a near-generalisation with a counterexample sharpens exactly what a rule does and doesn't claim.

activities.title: Check understanding with targeted questions
steps: Answer 'which known facts can you combine to make 8×7?' and explain why your choice works.
Sort a set of numbers into multiples of 4 and not-multiples-of-4, including an even non-multiple to catch over-generalising.
Spot the unreasonable answer: given candidate products, identify one that breaks a pattern (e.g. an odd 'multiple of 8') and say which pattern it breaks.
activities.insight: Questions can check both the derivation route and the pattern-as-check habit, including whether a child is fooled by a plausible wrong split; this checks recognition and stated reasoning, not whether the child can construct the derivation unprompted.

checkQuestion: You're sure that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16. Use those to work out 8 × 7 without counting up in eights. Then — how could you quickly check your answer looks sensible?
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for deriving 8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2 = 56, AND a reasonableness check such as '56 is even, and multiples of 8 (or 4) are even, so it looks right', or noticing it lies between 8×5 and 8×8. The derivation plus the self-check is the target.
